body_markdown:
There’s nothing quite so rewarding as reaching the summit of an effort into which we’ve put all-consuming amounts of time and emotion. Anybody who’s been at this hobby long enough has a thing or two to show for it, but if you’re anything like us, there’s always something on the horizon.


These are just a few of the items our team wants to cross off our lists. Let us know yours in the comments below.


## Cross-Country Solo Trip


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


I can be a bit of a loner sometimes, and recharging usually means being by myself for a bit. Often in a car, often with the top down and no specific heading. One day, I’d like to cross the country—still haven’t done that yet—solo, with no plan and no hurry. Just me, roads I choose off a paper map, and the towns along the way. I’ll send my people some postcards whenever I get to the Pacific. — *Eddy Eckart*


## A Full-on Restoration


McPherson College


Two years ago an[engine swap](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/my-ls-swapped-corvette-returns-to-jackstands/) was the top of this list for me, so I surprisingly find myself kinda flat-footed on this one.


I guess the top of the list has always been a full concours restoration. The paint and chalk marks, all the hardware, the whole nine. I don’t even know what car or truck I would want to do this adventure with, but the idea of not only learning all the correct details but being able to duplicate them decades removed from the original build seems like a mountain that would be a fun challenge to climb. Or it would drive me insane. Only one way to find out. — *Kyle Smith*


## Building an Engine


Kyle Kinard


I’ve always been intrigued by the concept of building an engine. Getting it fitted to a stand, pulling it all apart, redoing pieces that need love, reassembling it, and finally, installing it back under the hood.


Someday, I’d love to go from failure to flyer on an engine in a car that I own. Be the one behind the wheel when something goes catastrophically wrong, sit in that frustration, then knuckle down and prepare for the long road ahead. I’ll use problem-solving skills to figure out what went wrong, then start to plot a path forward to come back better than before. Hopefully the blowup wasn’t so bad that I need a donor engine, but if it comes to that, so be it.


I’ll put new bearings in, maybe new pushrods or cams, and slowly but surely, after many (probably too many) nights in the garage, bring something back to life. — *Nathan Petroelje*


## Trails. All of Them.


Maybe Kyle will lend Stefan his KTM…


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


Welp, since I’ll never realize my dream of being a gentleman racer at Le Mans in the 1950s and ’60s, my close second would be to drive all 15[Backcountry Discovery Routes](https://ridebdr.com/bdr-routes/) in the U.S. After doing[the Washington route](https://www.hagerty.com/media/great-reads/a-crusty-first-gen-nissan-xterra-takes-man-and-mans-best-friend-off-the-beaten-path/) and learning more about the entire system and the work that goes into planning and mapping them all, I think devoting a couple of years to tackling every one of them would be a spectacular way to see the country. And since they are primarily devised as motorcycle routes, I’d want to try at least one of them on a bike, which I should probably learn to ride first… — *Stefan Lombard*


## Closing the Circle


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


I’ve made a decent career out of looking for the next interesting thing to do, or the next interesting person to interview. By any measure (except for salary…) I’ve been pretty successful at having journalism actually pay for what I’d consider to be some sort of accomplishments, from attending almost all the races on my wish list, to topping 300 mph in a jet-powered truck, to suffering oxygen deprivation at 16,420 feet on a mountain road through the Andes, to driving from Anchorage to Prudhoe Bay in Alaska and back, alone and non-stop. So what automotive accomplishment is left? A comparatively modest one, perhaps: Years ago, I bought a 5.0-liter, Fox Body Ford Mustang race car. I knew what series I wanted to race in, what tracks I’d go to. Then I got laid off. Then my wife got really, really sick. And life happened. Through it all, the Mustang never made it off the trailer. Still hasn’t. It’s not fair to the car, which has been patiently waiting. When the weather cools off, I intend to roll it into the garage and work on it, beginning with replacing everything that’s liquid or made of rubber. Then we’ll see. I have a friend who owns a racetrack nearby, and I really want to take the car out, even for just a few laps. Closing a circle, I guess, that grew wider year after year. — *Steven Cole Smith*


## Standing on the Steps


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


A podium finish. I’ve been racing in EnduroKA for almost four years now and have come so, so close. Fourth in two 24-hour races, running third with 60 minutes to go in a 12-hour before the gearbox packed in. As a team we’ve really focused on strategy, pit work and our driving, but so far we haven’t quite made it onto the rostrum. I’ve got two races to go this season—wish me luck. — *Nik Berg*
